title: Monochoria vaginalis: How to Spot and Control Gabi Gabi in Rice
metaTitle: Monochoria vaginalis in Rice Fields: Spot It and Control It
metaDescription: Monochoria vaginalis, or gabi gabi, can cut palay yield by 25 percent. Learn to spot its heart shaped leaves and stop it early in your field.
excerpt: Monochoria vaginalis is a shiny, soft broadleaf weed that farmers call gabi gabi, because its heart shaped leaves look like small taro leaves. It grows in both irrigated and rainfed lowland rice fields across the Philippines. On this page, you will learn how to spot it early, how much it can cost your palay, and how to control it before it spreads.

blocks.text:
Monochoria vaginalis goes by gabi gabi or gabi gabihan in many barangays. It is a fleshy, semi aquatic plant from the water hyacinth family, Pontederiaceae. It is a monocot, but it sits in the broadleaf group because its leaves are wide and heart shaped, not thin like grass blades. Since it loves wet, muddy soil, you find it in irrigated and rainfed lowland rice fields.

Most plants live for one season, but some survive longer and act as perennials. It spreads by seeds and by small tubers in the soil. Its seeds also do not sprout all at once. Some come up early, while others wait in the mud and come up later. That is why one round of weeding rarely clears it for the whole season.

blocks.caption: Quick facts about Monochoria vaginalis
rows: Irrigated and rainfed lowland rice fields

blocks.text: Look for a shiny, soft plant standing in the water between your rice hills. Its stems are soft and upright, and they send out roots at the nodes. The leaves have a heart shape and sit on soft, hollow leaf stalks. Unlike grasses and sedges, it has wide leaves, but its veins curve along the leaf instead of forming a net. When it flowers, long stalks carry lilac blue or violet flowers in small groups.

items: Shiny, soft plants standing in the water between rice hills, glossy even from a distance.
Heart shaped leaves on soft, hollow stalks that look like tiny gabi leaves.
Soft, upright stems that send out roots wherever a node touches the mud.
Long flower stalks carrying lilac blue or violet flowers in small groups of 2 to 6.
New seedlings that keep coming up weeks after your last round of weeding.

blocks.text:
Gabi gabi may look harmless, but it fights your palay for light, water and fertilizer. At 100 plants per square meter, competing with rice from day 7 to day 40, it cut rice yield by 16 percent. When the same number of plants stayed until the crop matured, the loss climbed to 25 percent.

It is a C3 plant, and its seeds do not all sprout at the same time. Some come up early, while others wait. So a field that looks clean after one weeding can fill up again. That is how this weed slips past your control work and keeps stealing from your harvest.

items: Pull young plants by hand and lift out the base, because tubers left in the mud can sprout new plants.
Plan more than one round of weeding. Its seeds sprout at different times, so check the field again a few weeks after your first pass.
Remove plants before the violet flowers set seed, so fewer seeds drop into the mud for the next season.

blocks.text: What to Do at Each Age of Your Rice

items: **0 to 5 days:** keep the soil saturated. Use a pre emergence herbicide only if the field had many weeds last season.
**6 to 10 days:** hand weed in transplanted rice. In direct seeded rice, this is the window for an early post emergence spray.
**11 to 20 days:** keep water in the field, weed by hand or with a rotary weeder, and let Azolla and the Altica beetle help. Spray only if those fail.
**21 to 30 days:** top up the water and keep weeding. Spray only if weeding fails.
**31 to 40 days (transplanted rice):** hand weed. A spray this late is only a rescue.
After any post emergence spray, bring the water back within 1 to 3 days at 3 to 5 cm and hold it for 4 to 5 days. Keep young rice above it.

blocks.text: Active Ingredients That Work on Broadleaves

If water and weeding cannot hold Monochoria vaginalis down, choose an active ingredient that works on broadleaves at the age of your rice. The table follows PhilRice recommendations. Shop by the ingredient on the label, never by the brand. If your field also has other kinds of weeds, the [weed control helper](/weeds#control) finds the ingredients that cover all of them.

blocks.text: Use only herbicides registered with the [Fertilizer and Pesticide Authority](/blog/fertilizer-and-pesticide-authority), and follow the label on the pack: the rate, the timing, the water and the protective clothing. Switch herbicide groups between seasons so the weeds do not learn to survive them. Our [guide to herbicides for rice](/weeds/herbicides-for-rice-weeds) explains the groups.
Keep Monochoria vaginalis Out Next Season

items: Plant clean, certified seed. Weed seeds mixed into the punla are the easiest way in.
Keep the seedbed, the canals and the bunds free of weeds, so seed does not wash or blow into the paddy.
Plow and harrow well, and rake out the runners, roots or pieces you turn up. A small piece left in wet soil can grow a new plant.
Pull escapes before they flower and set seed, and carry them out of the paddy instead of leaving them on the bund.
Keep the field clean after harvest and through the fallow, so fewer seeds build up in the soil for next season.

blocks.text: These steps work for every [broadleaf weed](/weeds/types-of-weeds) in the paddy, not only this one. The [weed management guide](/weeds/weed-management-in-rice) puts them in order for a whole season.
Not Sure It Is Monochoria vaginalis?

Take a clear photo of the leaf, the stem and the flower or seed head, then ask [Anee, the smart farm technician](/features/ai-agricultural-technician) in anee.io, in Tagalog or English. Anee tells you which weed it most likely is, its group, and what to do at the age of your rice. blocks.text: Questions Farmers Ask About Monochoria vaginalis

items.q: What is Monochoria vaginalis called in Tagalog?
items.a: Many farmers call Monochoria vaginalis gabi gabi or gabi gabihan, because its heart shaped leaves look like small gabi or taro leaves. In English, it goes by heartshape false pickerelweed. If you hear any of these names in your barangay, they all point to the same shiny broadleaf weed of wet, lowland rice fields.

items.q: How do I control gabi gabi in my rice field?
items.a: Start with a clean field and good land preparation. Water will not stop it, since it loves wet soil. So hand weed early, and pull the whole plant with its base so no tubers stay behind. Check again later, because new seedlings keep coming. If you use a herbicide, choose one by weed group and the age of your rice, and always follow the FPA registered label.

items.q: Why does gabi gabi keep coming back after weeding?
items.a: Its seeds do not all sprout at the same time. Some germinate early, and others wait in the mud and come up weeks later. It can also grow back from tubers left in the soil. So one weeding is rarely enough. Plan two or more rounds, and remove the plants before they flower and drop seed.
